brief: Goldman splits the post-midterm AI trade into builders and owners. State moratoria (Goldman estimates roughly 45% of planned US capacity at risk, with Georgia, Ohio and Michigan copying Texas) threaten the 72 S&P 500 names selling into the data center buildout; those stocks fell 13.3% in two days versus a 1.7% gain for the five hyperscalers that own existing compute, even as the sellers' forward earnings estimates rose more than 50% relative to the market and their valuation hit its cheapest level since 2022. Goldman's Wilson argues the moratorium works like a moat: scarcer future supply raises pricing power and cuts capex for incumbent owners, illustrated by Microsoft reallocating capacity away from Oracle and Goldman's baskets desk recommending a hyperscaler-rebound call spread. Separately, credit barely reacted to Thursday's 4.4% equity selloff (investment-grade spreads widened only 2.2bps versus 8.2bps expected), which Goldman attributes to the selloff hitting capex spenders rather than bond-issuing recipients. But Goldman's own credit desk is positioned for spreads to widen anyway, since YTD hyperscaler issuance of $296 billion already exceeds assumptions, 2027 issuance is forecast larger still, and junk-rated AI debt has already cracked. Zero Hedge sides with that caution, calling the calm complacency rather than strength.
